Methodological Notes: Keywords were extracted from the verbatim Defined Objectives text after removing URLs, non-alphanumeric characters, and common stopwords. This ensured the retention of only substantive thematic terms. Keywords were compared against an iteratively developed lexicon covering ten high-level representative strategies (Governance & Planning, Financial Stewardship, Policy & Regulation, Environmental Action, Knowledge & Data, Innovation & Technology, Inclusion & Rights, Partnerships & Networks, Operational Delivery, Monitoring & Accountability). The lexicon was informed by United Nations frameworks, international policy instruments, and academic literature on institutional mandates. Candidate categories were first assigned through lexical matching (data-led) and then validated in context using KWIC evidence. The final mapping reflects an inductive process aligning empirical patterns with globally recognised strategic domains.

Institution: Division for Ocean Affairs and the Law of the Sea (UN DOALOS)
Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to the Secretary-General’s bulletin ST/SGB/2015/3, DOALOS's objectives encompass several key functions: promoting understanding of the UNCLOS and related Agreements, as well as aiding in their uniform application (Section 9.2 a); providing extensive support to meetings concerning the Convention, focusing on sustainable management of marine resources and dispute resolution (Section 9.2 c); assisting the Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf with technical aid for delineating continental shelf boundaries (Section 9.2 e); and supporting the General Assembly in matters of ocean and maritime law, including policy guidance and reporting on developments (Section 9.2 g) (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/798635/files/ST_SGB_2015_3-EN.pdf?ln=en). Additionally, DOALOS offers substantial support to the Review Conference on the UNFSA and consultations of States parties to that Agreement, and provides policy recommendations to support General Assembly resolutions on ocean affairs and sustainable fisheries ((https://www.un.org/oceancapacity/sites/www.un.org.oceancapacity/files/files/Projects/UNFSA/docs/unfsa_text-eng.pdf). This multifaceted role ensures the effective implementation of legal frameworks pertaining to ocean governance.

Methodological Notes: Keywords were extracted from the verbatim Defined Objectives text after removing URLs, non-alphanumeric characters, and common stopwords. This ensured the retention of only substantive thematic terms. Keywords were compared against an iteratively developed lexicon covering ten high-level representative strategies (Governance & Planning, Financial Stewardship, Policy & Regulation, Environmental Action, Knowledge & Data, Innovation & Technology, Inclusion & Rights, Partnerships & Networks, Operational Delivery, Monitoring & Accountability). Defined Objectives (verbatim): The secretariat's duties under the Convention include organizing and servicing sessions of the Conference of the Parties and its subsidiary bodies (Article 8, paragraph 2 (a)); compiling and transmitting reports from Parties and other sources, and supporting technical and financial assistance to Parties, particularly developing countries, for Convention compliance (Article 8, paragraphs 2 (b), (c), and 7); preparing and presenting activity reports to the Conference of the Parties and coordinating with relevant international organizations (Article 8, paragraphs 2 (d) and (e)); handling administrative and contractual arrangements as directed by the Conference of the Parties for effective functioning (Article 8, paragraph 2 (f)); and executing other specified secretariat roles in the Convention, its protocols, and tasks assigned by the Conference of the Parties (Article 8, paragraph 2 (g)). These responsibilities are key to ensuring effective implementation and coordination within the Convention's framework. (https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf)

Methodological Notes: Keywords were extracted from the verbatim Defined Objectives text after removing URLs, non-alphanumeric characters, and common stopwords. This ensured the retention of only substantive thematic terms. Keywords were compared against an iteratively developed lexicon covering ten high-level representative strategies (Governance & Planning, Financial Stewardship, Policy & Regulation, Environmental Action, Knowledge & Data, Innovation & Technology, Inclusion & Rights, Partnerships & Networks, Operational Delivery, Monitoring & Accountability). The lexicon was informed by United Nations frameworks, international policy instruments, and academic literature on institutional mandates. Candidate categories were first assigned through lexical matching (data-led) and then validated in context using KWIC evidence. The final mapping reflects an inductive process aligning empirical patterns with globally recognised strategic domains.

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Part XI, Section 4 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, the International Seabed Authority's objectives encompass several key functions: organizing and controlling activities in the Area, particularly with a view to administering the resources of the Area (Article 157, paragraph 1); establishing specific policies for the Authority in conformity with the Convention and the general policies established by the Assembly (Article 162, paragraph 1); adopting and applying provisionally the rules, regulations and procedures of the Authority relating to prospecting, exploration and exploitation in the Area, as well as the financial management and internal administration of the Authority (Article 162, paragraph 2 o); supervising and coordinating the implementation of the provisions of Part XI and inviting the attention of the Assembly to cases of non-compliance (Article 162, paragraph 2 a); exercising control over activities in the Area in accordance with Article 153, paragraph 4, and the rules, regulations and procedures of the Authority (Article 162, paragraph 2 l); and ensuring the equitable sharing of financial and other economic benefits derived from activities in the Area, taking into account the interests and needs of developing States and peoples who have not attained full independence or other self-governing status (Article 160, paragraph 2 f and g; Article 162, paragraph 2 g). These functions enable the Authority to fulfil its role as the organization through which States Parties shall carry out their rights and obligations under the Convention with respect to activities in the Area (https://www.un.org/depts/los/convention_agreements/texts/unclos/part11-4.htm).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to the Governing Council decision 2/1 of 15 June 1972, the UNEP’s objectives encompass several key functions: providing general policy guidance for the direction and coordination of environmental programmes within the United Nations system (paragraph 2 a); keeping under review the world environmental situation in order to ensure that emerging environmental problems of wide international significance receive appropriate and adequate consideration by Governments (paragraph 2 b); promoting international cooperation in the field of the environment and recommending, as appropriate, policies to this end (paragraph 2 c); providing assistance to developing countries and regions in the implementation of environmental programmes and policies (paragraph 2 d); and initiating and coordinating scientific research and technological development in the field of the environment (paragraph 2 e) (https://documents-dds-ny.un.org/doc/RESOLUTION/GEN/NR0/270/27/IMG/NR027027.pdf?OpenElement). Additionally, UNEP is responsible for disseminating information and raising public awareness on environmental issues, facilitating the exchange of information and experience among countries, and providing advisory services and technical assistance to Governments and intergovernmental bodies on environmental matters (https://www.unep.org/news-and-stories). These functions enable UNEP to fulfil its role as the leading global authority on the environment and the principal advocate for environmental action within the United Nations system (https://www.unep.org/who-we-are/about-us).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): As per the  General Assembly resolution 1995 (XIX) of 30 December 1964 (https://unctad.org/system/files/official-document/edmmisc232add19_en.pdf),  Key objectives of UNCTAD include promoting international trade, especially to accelerate economic development, and enhancing trade between countries at varied development stages, including developing countries and those with different economic systems (section II, paragraph 3 a). It formulates principles and policies on international trade and economic development (section II, paragraph 3 b), proposes effective implementation strategies, considering economic system diversity and development stages (section II, paragraph 3 c). UNCTAD reviews and coordinates United Nations system activities in international trade and economic development, collaborating with the General Assembly and Economic and Social Council (section II, paragraph 3 d). It initiates actions for negotiating and adopting multilateral trade legal instruments (section II, paragraph 3 e), harmonizes trade and development policies of governments and regional groups (section II, paragraph 3 f), and addresses other relevant matters (section II, paragraph 3 g). Additionally, UNCTAD evaluates and recommends institutional arrangement improvements, including comprehensive organization establishment within the UN system (section III, paragraphs 30 and 31). These functions establish UNCTAD as the General Assembly's principal organ in trade and development (section I, paragraph 1).

Methodological Notes: Keywords were extracted from the verbatim Defined Objectives text after removing URLs, non-alphanumeric characters, and common stopwords. This ensured the retention of only substantive thematic terms. Keywords were compared against an iteratively developed lexicon covering ten high-level representative strategies (Governance & Planning, Financial Stewardship, Policy & Regulation, Environmental Action, Knowledge & Data, Innovation & Technology, Inclusion & Rights, Partnerships & Networks, Operational Delivery, Monitoring & Accountability). The lexicon was informed by United Nations frameworks, international policy instruments, and academic literature on institutional mandates. Candidate categories were first assigned through lexical matching (data-led) and then validated in context using KWIC evidence. The final mapping reflects an inductive process aligning empirical patterns with globally recognised strategic domains.

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Chapter I of the Constitution of the UNIDO, the Organization's objectives are to promote and accelerate industrial development in the developing countries, with a view to assisting in the establishment of a new international economic order, and to promote industrial development and cooperation on global, regional and national, as well as on sectoral levels (Article 1). To fulfil these objectives, the Organization shall perform various functions, such as encouraging and assisting the developing countries in their industrialization efforts, initiating and coordinating the activities of the United Nations system in the field of industrial development, creating and developing new concepts and approaches for industrial development, providing a forum and an instrument for international cooperation and dialogue on industrial matters, serving as a clearing-house for industrial information, promoting and encouraging the development, transfer and use of industrial technology, organizing and supporting industrial training programmes, assisting in the exploitation, conservation and transformation of natural resources, developing special measures for the least-developed and other disadvantaged developing countries, and assisting in obtaining external financing for industrial projects (Article 2). These functions enable the Organization to play the central role in and be responsible for reviewing and promoting the coordination of all activities of the United Nations system in the field of industrial development, in conformity with the responsibilities of the Economic and Social Council under the Charter of the United Nations and with the applicable relationship agreements (https://www.unido.org/sites/default/files/files/2020-11/19-12162_UNIDO_Constitution_ebook.pdf).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to the Preamble and Chapter I of the ILO Constitution, the International Labour Organization's objectives encompass several key principles: promoting social justice and internationally recognized human and labour rights, based on the Declaration of Philadelphia and the Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work (Preamble); establishing and adopting international labour standards in the form of Conventions and Recommendations, and ensuring their effective observance by the Members (Article 19, Article 22, Article 23, Article 24, Article 26); fostering cooperation among the Members and with other international organizations, especially the United Nations, in the fields of industry and employment (Article 12, Article 13); and providing technical assistance, information, and publications on various aspects of industrial life and labour (Article 10, Article 11) (https://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---asia/---ro-bangkok/---ilo-hanoi/documents/publication/wcms_818973.pdf). These principles enable the Organization to fulfil its role as the specialized agency of the United Nations devoted to promoting rights at work, creating greater opportunities for women and men to decent employment and income, enhancing the coverage and effectiveness of social protection for all, and strengthen tripartism and social dialogue  (https://www.ilo.org/global/about-the-ilo/mission-and-objectives/lang--en/index.htm).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): ITU, per its Constitution (Chapter I, Article 1), pursues objectives to enhance telecommunication globally. These include maintaining international cooperation for telecommunication improvements (Article 1, paragraph 2 a), enhancing participation and fostering partnerships between entities and Member States (Article 1, paragraph 2 abis), offering technical assistance to developing countries and mobilizing resources for telecommunications (Article 1, paragraph 2 b), developing technical facilities for efficient telecommunication services (Article 1, paragraph 2 c), extending new telecommunication technologies worldwide (Article 1, paragraph 2 d), using telecommunications to facilitate peaceful relations (Article 1, paragraph 2 e), harmonizing Member States' actions and promoting cooperation (Article 1, paragraph 2 f), and adopting a broader approach to telecommunication issues in cooperation with other organizations (Article 1, paragraph 2 g) (https://www.itu.int/en/council/Documents/basic-texts/Constitution-E.pdf). These objectives establish ITU as the UN's specialized agency for telecommunications, contributing to global information society development.

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to the Preamble and Part I of the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the objectives of the UNICEF have been mandated to fulfil, as specified in this document, include several key functions: promoting and protecting the rights of every child, in accordance with the principles proclaimed in the Charter of the United Nations and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Preamble, paragraph 2); ensuring that each child enjoys a full and decent life, in conditions that ensure dignity, promote self-reliance and facilitate the child's active participation in the community (Article 23, paragraph 1); providing appropriate assistance and protection to children who are living in exceptionally difficult conditions, such as those affected by armed conflict, disability, displacement, exploitation, abuse or neglect (Preamble, paragraph 9; Article 22, 23, 32, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39); respecting the responsibilities, rights and duties of parents or other persons legally responsible for the child, and providing them with the necessary support for the child's well-being and development (Article 5, 18, 27); and fostering international cooperation for improving the living conditions of children in every country, in particular in the developing countries (Preamble, paragraph 10; Article 4, 17, 23, 24, 28, 29, 45) (https://www.unicef.org/media/52626/file). These functions enable the UNICEF to fulfil its role as the United Nations Children's Fund, which is responsible for providing humanitarian and developmental aid to children worldwide (https://www.unicef.org/what-we-do).

Methodological Notes: Keywords were extracted from the verbatim Defined Objectives text after removing URLs, non-alphanumeric characters, and common stopwords. This ensured the retention of only substantive thematic terms. Keywords were compared against an iteratively developed lexicon covering ten high-level representative strategies (Governance & Planning, Financial Stewardship, Policy & Regulation, Environmental Action, Knowledge & Data, Innovation & Technology, Inclusion & Rights, Partnerships & Networks, Operational Delivery, Monitoring & Accountability). Candidate categories were first assigned through lexical matching (data-led) and then validated in context using KWIC evidence. The final mapping reflects an inductive process aligning empirical patterns with globally recognised strategic domains.

Defined Objectives (verbatim): WHO's objective, as per its Constitution (Chapter I, Article 1), is the attainment of the highest possible health level for all peoples. Its functions include acting as the authority on international health work (Article 2 a), establishing collaboration with the UN, specialized agencies, and health administrations (Article 2 b), assisting governments in strengthening health services (Article 2 c and d), conducting health research and establishing standards (Article 2 n, s, and t), improving teaching and training standards in health-related professions (Article 2 o), studying and reporting on public health techniques (Article 2 p), providing health information and assistance (Article 2 q and r), proposing health-related conventions and recommendations (Article 2 k), and taking actions to further its objectives (Article 2 v). These roles position WHO as a specialized agency within the United Nations system, primarily responsible for international health matters and public health (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Treaties/1948/04/19480407%2010-51%20PM/Ch_IX_01p.pdf)

Defined Objectives (verbatim): OHCHR, as mandated by General Assembly Resolution 48/141, aims to promote and protect all human rights. Its objectives include promoting all civil, cultural, economic, political, and social rights (paragraph 4 a), carrying out tasks assigned by UN bodies in human rights and making recommendations (paragraph 4 b), promoting the right to development and enhancing support from UN bodies (paragraph 4 c), providing advisory services and technical and financial assistance to support human rights actions and programs (paragraph 4 d), coordinating UN education and public information programmes in human rights (paragraph 4 e), actively working to remove obstacles and prevent human rights violations (paragraph 4 f), engaging in dialogue with governments for human rights implementation (paragraph 4 g), enhancing international cooperation for human rights promotion and protection (paragraph 4 h), coordinating human rights activities across the UN system (paragraph 4 i), streamlining the UN human rights machinery for improved efficiency (paragraph 4 j), and overseeing the Centre for Human Rights (paragraph 4 k). These roles establish the OHCHR as the key UN entity responsible for human rights activities under the Secretary-General's direction. Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030, the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) has been mandated to fulfil several objectives (https://www.preventionweb.net/files/43291_sendaiframeworkfordrren.pdf?_gl=1*2d1si0*_ga*Nzc0NjIwODE4LjE3MDM1ODgxNDM.*_ga_D8G5WXP6YM*MTcwMzU4ODE1Mi4xLjEuMTcwMzU5MTQ1NC4wLjAuMA..), such as: supporting the implementation, follow-up and review of the Framework, including through the development of coherent and actionable guidance for its implementation (paragraph 49 a); supporting the coordination of disaster risk reduction in the United Nations system (paragraph 49 b); supporting the coherence of the disaster risk reduction and climate change agendas (paragraph 49 c); convening the Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction and supporting the organization of regional platforms for disaster risk reduction (paragraph 49 d); supporting the development of national and local disaster risk reduction strategies and plans, and facilitating their integration into relevant development and sectoral plans and policies (paragraph 49 e); supporting the development and strengthening of national and local mechanisms and capacities for monitoring and reviewing progress and levels of implementation of the Framework (paragraph 49 f); and supporting the development of indicators and methodologies for the assessment of disaster risk and disaster risk reduction (paragraph 49 g). These objectives enable the UNDRR to fulfil its role as the focal point in the United Nations system for the coordination of disaster risk reduction and the implementation of the Framework (https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/migration/generalassembly/docs/globalcompact/A_RES_69_283.pdf).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), as stated in Article II of its Statute (https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/statute.pdf), aims to accelerate and enlarge atomic energy's contribution to peace, health, and prosperity worldwide while ensuring no assistance is used for military purposes. Its key functions include encouraging research and practical application of atomic energy for peaceful uses (Article III, paragraph A 1), providing materials, services, and facilities for atomic energy development and application, focusing on under-developed areas (Article III, paragraph A 2), fostering the exchange of scientific information and training in peaceful atomic energy uses (Article III, paragraphs A 3 and 4), establishing safeguards against atomic energy's use for military purposes (Article III, paragraph A 5), setting safety standards for health protection and danger minimization (Article III, paragraph A 6), and acquiring facilities for carrying out its functions (Article III, paragraph A 7). These roles establish the IAEA as a key international organization promoting peaceful nuclear energy use and preventing its militarization (https://www.iaea.org/about/overview).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Part II, Article 2 of the Convention of the World Meteorological Organization (https://library.wmo.int/viewer/48992/download?file=15_2021_en.pdf&type=pdf&navigator=1). The objectives encompass six main purposes: facilitating worldwide cooperation in the establishment and maintenance of networks of stations and centres for meteorological, hydrological and related observations and services (Article 2 a); promoting the establishment and maintenance of systems for the rapid exchange of meteorological and related information (Article 2 b); promoting standardization of meteorological and related observations and ensuring the uniform publication of observations and statistics (Article 2 c); furthering the application of meteorology to aviation, shipping, water problems, agriculture and other human activities (Article 2 d); promoting activities in operational hydrology and furthering close cooperation between Meteorological and Hydrological Services (Article 2 e); and encouraging research and training in meteorology and, as appropriate, in related fields and assisting in coordinating the international aspects of such research and training (Article 2 f). These purposes enable the WMO to fulfil its role as the specialized agency of the United Nations for meteorology, operational hydrology and related geophysical sciences (https://library.wmo.int/doc_num.php?explnum_id=11187).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Article 1 of the Convention on the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the OECD's objectives encompass several key aims: achieving the highest sustainable economic growth and employment and a rising standard of living in member countries, while maintaining financial stability, and thus contributing to the development of the world economy (Article 1 a); contributing to sound economic expansion in member as well as non-member countries in the process of economic development (Article 1 b); and contributing to the expansion of world trade on a multilateral, non-discriminatory basis in accordance with international obligations (Article 1 c) (https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20888/volume-888-I-12736-English.pdf). These aims enable the OECD to fulfil its role as an intergovernmental organisation that works to build better policies for better lives, providing a platform to compare policy experiences, seek answers to common problems, identify good practices, and coordinate domestic and international policies of its members (https://www.oecd.org/about/).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): The objectives of the WBG are established in the Articles of Agreement and Conventions of its constituent institutions (https://www.worldbank.org/en/about/articles-of-agreement). The IBRD Articles of Agreement (https://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/722361541184234501/IBRDArticlesOfAgreement-English.pdf) state that the WBG through IBRD aims to assist in the reconstruction and development of territories of members by facilitating the investment of capital for productive purposes, promoting private foreign investment by means of guarantees or participations in loans and other investments, and supplementing private investment by providing finance for productive purposes out of its own capital, funds raised by it and its other resources (Article I, Section 1). As specified in the IDA Articles of Agreement (https://ida.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/pdfs/ida-articlesofagreement.pdf), the WBG through IDA aims to promote economic development, increase productivity and thus raise standards of living in the less-developed areas of the world by providing finance to projects and programs that contribute to the economic or social development of the members whose per capita income is low, and to those members in the opinion of the Association are not able to borrow from the IBRD on suitable terms (Article I, Section 1). The WBG through the IFC Articles of Agreement (https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/6a4a091b83577eb35e881dbf9016c5c3-0330032020/original/IFCArticlesOfAgreement.pdf) aims to further economic development by encouraging the growth of productive private enterprise in member countries, particularly in the less-developed areas, by assisting in financing the establishment, improvement and expansion of private productive enterprises, and by stimulating and helping to create conditions conducive to the flow of private capital, domestic and foreign, into productive investment in member countries (Article I, Section 1). According to the MIGA Convention (https://www.miga.org/sites/default/files/archive/Documents/miga_convention_november_2010.pdf), the WBG through MIGA aims to encourage the flow of investments for productive purposes among member countries, and in particular to developing member countries, by providing guarantees against non-commercial risks in respect of investments in member countries, by establishing and operating a trust fund to provide technical assistance to member countries in connection with the promotion of foreign investment, and by exercising such other incidental powers as shall be necessary or desirable in the furtherance of its objective (Article 2, Section 1). Lastly, the WBG through the ICSID Convention (https://icsid.worldbank.org/sites/default/files/ICSID%20Convention%20English.pdf) aims to provide facilities for conciliation and arbitration of investment disputes between contracting states and nationals of other contracting states, and to bring together parties who have agreed to use such facilities, in order to facilitate the settlement of such disputes and to contribute to the development of international law on investments (Article 1, Section 2).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Article I of the Articles of Agreement of the IMF (https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/aa/pdf/aa.pdf), the IMF's objectives cover several key areas: promoting international monetary cooperation through a permanent institution that provides the machinery for consultation and collaboration on international monetary problems (Objective i); facilitating the expansion and balanced growth of international trade, and contributing thereby to the promotion and maintenance of high levels of employment and real income and to the development of the productive resources of all members as primary objectives of economic policy (Objective ii); promoting exchange stability, maintaining orderly exchange arrangements among members, and avoiding competitive exchange depreciation (Objective iii); assisting in the establishment of a multilateral system of payments in respect of current transactions between members and in the elimination of foreign exchange restrictions which hamper the growth of world trade (Objective iv); giving confidence to members by making the general resources of the Fund temporarily available to them under adequate safeguards, thus providing them with opportunity to correct maladjustments in their balance of payments without resorting to measures destructive of national or international prosperity (Objective v); and in accordance with the above, shortening the duration and lessening the degree of disequilibrium in the international balances of payments of members (Objective vi).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Article II f the IHO Convention (https://iho.int/uploads/user/pubs/misc/M1_Separatedocs/Convention_new_EN.pdf), the International Hydrographic Organization's objectives cover several key areas: promoting the use of hydrography for the safety of navigation and all other marine purposes and raising global awareness of the importance of hydrography (Object a); improving global coverage, availability and quality of hydrographic data, information, products and services and facilitating access to such data, information, products and services (Object b); improving global hydrographic capability, capacity, training, science and techniques (Purpose, Object c); establishing and enhancing the development of international standards for hydrographic data, information, products, services and techniques and achieving the greatest possible uniformity in the use of these standards (Object d); giving authoritative and timely guidance on all hydrographic matters to States and international organizations (Object e); facilitating coordination of hydrographic activities among the Member States (Object f); and enhancing cooperation on hydrographic activities among States on a regional basis (Object g). These objectives enable the Organization to fulfil its vision of being the authoritative, worldwide hydrographic body that actively engages all coastal and interested states to advance maritime safety and efficiency and supports the protection and sustainable use of the marine environment.

Institution: International Council for the Exploration of the Sea (ICES)
Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to the Convention for the ICES (https://www.ices.dk/about-ICES/who-we-are/Documents/ICES_Convention_1964.pdf), the Council's objectives encompass three main duties: promoting and encouraging research and investigations for the study of the sea particularly those related to the living resources thereof (Article 1 a); drawing up programmes required for this purpose and organising, in agreement with the Contracting Parties, such research and investigation as may appear necessary (Article 1 b); and publishing or otherwise disseminating the results of research and investigations carried out under its auspices or to encourage the publication thereof (Article 1 c). Institution: The Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES)
Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to the Resolution on the IPBES during second session of Plenary in 2012 (https://www.ipbes.net/resource-file/2674), the overarching objective of the IPBES platform is to strengthen the science-policy interface for biodiversity and ecosystem services for the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity, long-term human well-being and sustainable development (Section I, Paragraph 1). Other functions of IPBES defined in the resolution include responding to requests from Governments and other stakeholders on biodiversity and ecosystem services issues (Section I, Paragraph 1a); identifying and prioritizing key scientific information needed for policymakers and catalysing efforts to generate new knowledge (Section I, Paragraph 1b); performing regular and timely assessments of knowledge on biodiversity and ecosystem services and their interlinkages (Section I, Paragraph 1c); supporting policy formulation and implementation by identifying policy-relevant tools and methodologies (Section I, Paragraph 1d); and prioritizing and providing capacity-building for the science-policy interface (Section I, Paragraph 1e).

Defined Objectives (verbatim):
As defined in Paragraph 2 of Resolution 4 (EC-XL) of the WMO Executive Council (https://archive.ipcc.ch/docs/WMO_resolution4_on_IPCC_1988.pdf), the IPCC's objectives include the following main tasks:
(1) Assessing the scientific information that is related to the various components of the climate change issue, such as emissions of major greenhouse gases and modification of the Earth's radiation balance resulting therefrom, and the environmental and socio-economic consequences of climate change; (2) Formulating realistic response strategies for the management of the climate change issue; (3) Providing scientific and socio-economic information and advice, initially for the development and negotiations of a UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and after its entry into force, to continue to work closely with the UNFCCC and provide scientific, technical and socio-economic information and advice; and (4) Reporting on its activities to the governing bodies of WMO and UNEP and communicating the results of the assessments broadly. These tasks enable the IPCC to fulfil its role as an intergovernmental panel on climate change that provides authoritative and comprehensive assessments of the current state of knowledge on climate change and its potential impacts.

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Article III of the Marrakesh Agreement Establishing the World Trade Organization (https://www.wto.org/english/docs_e/legal_e/04-wto.pdf), the WTO's objectives encompass several key functions: facilitating the implementation, administration and operation of the WTO agreements and providing a framework for their further negotiation (paragraph 1); providing a forum for trade negotiations and a framework for their implementation (paragraph 2); administering the dispute settlement mechanism and ensuring the prompt and effective resolution of trade disputes (paragraph 3); administering the trade policy review mechanism and enhancing the transparency of trade policies (paragraph 4); cooperating with other international organizations and ensuring greater coherence in global economic policy-making (paragraph 5); and helping developing countries, especially the least-developed ones, to benefit from the multilateral trading system and to achieve their trade and development objectives. These functions enable the WTO to fulfil its role as the common institutional framework for the conduct of trade relations among its members in matters related to the WTO agreements (Article II, paragraph 1).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Chapter I (Article 1) of the Constitution of the International Organization for Migration (https://publications.iom.int/system/files/pdf/iom-constitution-3rd-en.pdf), the defined purposes and functions of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) are: (1) To arrange the transfer of migrants who need special assistance or who lack adequate facilities to move to countries offering opportunities for orderly migration, (2) To provide migration services such as recruitment, selection, processing, language training, orientation, medical examination, placement, integration, and return migration, at the request and in agreement with the States concerned, (3) To provide a forum for cooperation and coordination on international migration issues, including studies, research and consultation, among States and other relevant actors, such as international organizations and civil society, (4) To cooperate closely with other international organizations concerned with migration, refugees and human resources, in order to facilitate the harmonization of international activities in these fields, and (5) To recognize the linkages between migration and other areas such as economic, social and cultural development, human rights, humanitarian assistance, and environmental sustainability.

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to the UNOPS strategic plan, 2022-2025 (https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3932593/files/DP_OPS_2021_5-EN.pdf?ln=en), the UNOPS objectives are based on three contribution goals which reflect its purpose, vision and mission. These goals aim to (1) Supports countries in developing their capacity and resource base for the Sustainable Development Goals, by applying its technical expertise in quality infrastructure, public procurement, and sustainable investments in infrastructure and innovation (paragraphs 50-80), (2) Help people in need through effective specialized expertise grounded in international norms and standards, by embedding sustainable, resilient and inclusive implementation approaches, and by learning from its operational experience (paragraphs 81-93), and (3) Enable UNOPS's partners to 'do more with less' through efficient project services, delivered locally or as global shared services, by offering flexible and modular service lines, integrated service offerings and specialized delivery modalities, and by pursuing quality and organizational excellence (paragraphs 94-104).

the empowerment of women; and the achievement of equality between women and men as partners and beneficiaries of development, human rights, humanitarian action and peace and security (Paragraph 5), (2) Lead and coordinate United Nations system efforts to ensure that commitments on gender equality and gender mainstreaming translate into action throughout the world (Paragraph 5), (3) Provide strong and coherent leadership in support of Member States’ priorities and efforts, building effective partnerships with civil society and other relevant actors (Paragraph 5), (4) Perform eight functions, as outlined in the Deputy Secretary-General’s papers of August 2007 and July 2008, which include providing substantive support to intergovernmental bodies, supporting national efforts through innovative and catalytic programming, undertaking advocacy on critical issues, supporting Member States in implementing and monitoring intergovernmental agreements, undertaking research and analytical work, leading and coordinating United Nations system strategies and actions, strengthening the accountability of the United Nations system, and monitoring and reporting on system-wide compliance with gender balance (Paragraphs 5-6), and (5) Add value by providing capacity to meet the need for a strong voice for women and girls at the global, regional and local levels; better support for Member States as they enhance the normative and policy environment for accelerating progress towards full equality for women and girls; assistance for national partners as they respond to critical gaps and challenges; and an enhanced United Nations response to the country-defined needs and priorities of women and girls (Paragraph 21).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to the Convention Establishing the World Intellectual Property Organization (https://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text/283833), WIPO's objectives encompass two main aspects: promoting the protection of intellectual property throughout the world (Article 3(i)) and ensuring administrative cooperation among the Unions (Article 3(ii)). To achieve these objectives, the Organization, through its appropriate organs, has several functions, such as: developing measures to facilitate the efficient protection of intellectual property and to harmonize national legislation in this field (Article 4(i)); performing the administrative tasks of the Paris Union, the Berne Union, and other international agreements related to intellectual property (Article 4(ii)); encouraging the conclusion of international agreements to promote the protection of intellectual property; offering legal-technical assistance to States requesting it (Article 4(iv)); assembling and disseminating information concerning the protection of intellectual property (Article 4(vi)); maintaining services facilitating the international protection of intellectual property (Article 4(vii)); and taking all other appropriate action in relation to the stated objectives (Article 4(viii)). These objectives and functions enable WIPO to contribute to better understanding and cooperation among States for their mutual benefit on the basis of respect for their sovereignty and equality, and to encourage creative activity in the industrial, scientific, literary or artistic fields (Preamble).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Article 3 of the Statutes of the UNWTO, the UNWTO's objectives are defined as (1) To promote and develop tourism as a significant means of fostering international peace and understanding, economic development and international trade (Article 3, paragraph 1), (2) To pay particular attention to the interests of the developing countries in the field of tourism (Article 3, paragraph 2), and (3) To establish and maintain effective collaboration with the appropriate organs of the United Nations and its specialized agencies (Article 3, paragraph 3). Institution: Secretariat of the Basel, Rotterdam and Stockholm Conventions (BRS)
Defined Objectives (verbatim): The BRS Secretariat's objectives encompass several key tasks: (1) Mobilizing resources and support for the implementation of the BRS Conventions programmes of work, including from the private sector and other relevant stakeholders, (2) Strengthening relationship and cooperation with other international bodies and the UN system on the sound management of hazardous chemicals and wastes, within the context of the global development agenda, (3) Enhancing science-based action and information sharing in the implementation of the BRS Conventions at the global, regional and national levels, (4) Developing and managing the technical assistance programme for the conventions, based on the needs assessment and capacity-building activities of the Parties, (5) Managing the development of technical documents, including guidelines and guidance, and facilitating the work of the scientific and technical subsidiary bodies of the conventions, and (6) Managing and coordinating the meetings of the conferences of the Parties and their subsidiary bodies, and providing legal and governance support, including on compliance, strategic issues and partnerships (https://www.brsmeas.org/Secretariat/Vision/Vision201819/tabid/7862/language/en-US/Default.aspx).

Institution: Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to the Convention on Biological Diversity (https://www.cbd.int/doc/legal/cbd-en.pdf), the CBD's objectives are to pursue the following goals in accordance with its relevant provisions: (1) Conservation of biological diversity: to protect and maintain the variability among living organisms and the ecological systems they form, as well as their intrinsic and instrumental values for humanity (preamble; Article 1), (2) Sustainable use of its components: to use the components of biological diversity, such as genetic resources, species and ecosystems, in a way and at a rate that does not lead to their long-term decline, thereby maintaining their potential to meet the needs and aspirations of present and future generations (preamble; Article 1), and (3) Fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising from the utilization of genetic resources: to ensure that the benefits derived from the access to and exploitation of genetic resources, such as scientific, technological, economic and social benefits, are shared in a fair and equitable way with the countries and communities that provide such resources, as well as with the holders of traditional knowledge, innovations and practices relevant to the conservation and sustainable use of biological diversity (preamble; Article 1; Article 8 j; Article 15; Article 16; Article 19). This objective also includes the provision of appropriate access to genetic resources and the transfer of relevant technologies, taking into account all rights over those resources and technologies (Article 1; Article 15; Article 16).

Institution: Secretariat of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES)
Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Article XII of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (https://cites.org/sites/default/files/eng/disc/CITES-Convention-EN.pdf), the CITES Secretariat's objectives include the following tasks: (1) To arrange for and service meetings of the Parties (paragraph 2 a); (2) To perform the functions entrusted to it under the provisions of Articles XV and XVI of the Convention, which relate to amendments to Appendices I and II and Appendix III and amendments thereto (paragraph 2 b); (3) To undertake scientific and technical studies in accordance with programmes authorized by the Conference of the Parties as will contribute to the implementation of the Convention, including studies concerning standards for appropriate preparation and shipment of living specimens and the means of identifying specimens (paragraph 2 c); (4) To study the reports of Parties and to request from Parties such further information with respect thereto as it deems necessary to ensure implementation of the Convention (paragraph 2 d); (5) To invite the attention of the Parties to any matter pertaining to the aims of the Convention (paragraph 2 e); (6) To publish and distribute to the Parties current editions of Appendices I, II and III together with any information which will facilitate identification of specimens of species included in those Appendices (paragraph 2 f); (7) To prepare annual reports to the Parties on its work and on the implementation of the Convention and such other reports as meetings of the Parties may request (paragraph 2 g); (8) To make recommendations for the implementation of the aims and provisions of the Convention, including the exchange of information of a scientific or technical nature (paragraph 2 h);and (9) To perform any other function as may be entrusted to it by the Parties (paragraph 2 i).

Methodological Notes: Keywords were extracted from the verbatim Defined Objectives text after removing URLs, non-alphanumeric characters, and common stopwords. This ensured the retention of only substantive thematic terms. Keywords were compared against an iteratively developed lexicon covering ten high-level representative strategies (Governance & Planning, Financial Stewardship, Policy & Regulation, Environmental Action, Knowledge & Data, Innovation & Technology, Inclusion & Rights, Partnerships & Networks, Operational Delivery, Monitoring & Accountability). The lexicon was informed by United Nations frameworks, international policy instruments, and academic literature on institutional mandates. Candidate categories were first assigned through lexical matching (data-led) and then validated in context using KWIC evidence. The final mapping reflects an inductive process aligning empirical patterns with globally recognised strategic domains.

Institution: Secretariat of the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS)
Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Article IX of the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (https://www.cms.int/sites/default/files/instrument/CMS-text.en_.PDF), the CMS Secretariat's objectives include several key functions: arranging for and servicing meetings of the Conference of the Parties, the Scientific Council and the Standing Committee (paragraph 4 a); maintaining liaison with and promoting liaison between the Parties, the standing bodies set up under AGREEMENTS and other international organizations concerned with migratory species (paragraph 4 b); obtaining from any appropriate source reports and other information which will further the objectives and implementation of this Convention and arranging for the appropriate dissemination of such information (paragraph 4 c); inviting the attention of the Conference of the Parties to any matter pertaining to the objectives of this Convention (paragraph 4 d); preparing for the Conference of the Parties reports on the work of the Secretariat and on the implementation of this Convention (paragraph 4 e); maintaining and publishing a list of Range States of all migratory species included in Appendices I and II (paragraph 4 f); promoting, under the direction of the Conference of the Parties, the conclusion of AGREEMENTS (paragraph 4 g); maintaining and making available to the Parties a list of AGREEMENTS and, if so required by the Conference of the Parties, providing any information on such AGREEMENTS (paragraph 4 h); maintaining and publishing a list of the recommendations made by the Conference of the Parties pursuant to subparagraphs (e), (f) and (g) of paragraph 5 of Article VII or of decisions made pursuant to sub-paragraph (h) of that paragraph (paragraph 4 i); providing for the general public information concerning this Convention and its objectives (paragraph 4 j); and performing any other function entrusted to it under this Convention or by the Conference of the Parties (paragraph 4 k). These functions enable the Secretariat to fulfil its role as the Convention's coordinating body.

Methodological Notes: Keywords were extracted from the verbatim Defined Objectives text after removing URLs, non-alphanumeric characters, and common stopwords. This ensured the retention of only substantive thematic terms. Keywords were compared against an iteratively developed lexicon covering ten high-level representative strategies (Governance & Planning, Financial Stewardship, Policy & Regulation, Environmental Action, Knowledge & Data, Innovation & Technology, Inclusion & Rights, Partnerships & Networks, Operational Delivery, Monitoring & Accountability). The lexicon was informed by United Nations frameworks, international policy instruments, and academic literature on institutional mandates. Candidate categories were first assigned through lexical matching (data-led) and then validated in context using KWIC evidence. The final mapping reflects an inductive process aligning empirical patterns with globally recognised strategic domains.

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Article 2 of the Agreement Establishing the International Fund for Agricultural Development (https://www.ifad.org/documents/38711624/39421015/agree_e.pdf/b06d3b8f-6fb5-4db1-8054-b1ef21d746a5), IFAD's objectives encompass several key functions: mobilizing additional resources to be made available on concessional terms for agricultural development in developing Member States (Article 2, paragraph 1); providing financing primarily for projects and programmes specifically designed to introduce, expand or improve food production systems and to strengthen related policies and institutions within the framework of national priorities and strategies (Article 2, paragraph 2); furnishing technical assistance and policy advice, as well as facilitating the access of developing Member States to technology and information, in support of the above-mentioned activities (Article 2, paragraph 3); and promoting and facilitating the participation of the rural poor, particularly women and youth, in the decisions and activities affecting their living conditions and well-being (Article 2, paragraph 4). These functions enable the Fund to fulfil its role as an international financial institution and a specialized agency of the United Nations dedicated to eradicating rural poverty in developing countries (https://www.ifad.org/en/vision).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Article 23 of the UNCCD Convention (https://catalogue.unccd.int/936_UNCCD_Convention_ENG.pdf), the UNCCD Secretariat's objectives encompass several key functions: making arrangements for sessions of the Conference of the Parties (COP) and its subsidiary bodies established under the Convention, and providing them with services as required (Article 23, paragraph 1); compiling and transmitting reports submitted to it (Article 23, paragraph 2); facilitating assistance to affected developing country Parties, on request, particularly those in Africa, in the compilation and communication of information required under the Convention (Article 23, paragraph 3); and coordinating its activities with the secretariats of other relevant international bodies and conventions (Article 23, paragraph 4). Additionally, according to the UNCCD 2018-2030 Strategic Framework, the UNCCD Secretariat's objectives also include: acting as an advocate for land, ensuring land-related issues are put front and center on the development agenda; championing for healthy, productive and accessible land around the world; supporting countries in achieving land degradation neutrality, integrating strategies for poverty eradication, and promoting cooperation among affected country Parties; and providing access to the latest data and knowledge, ensuring that best practices are shared and opportunities for capacity-building are increased. These functions enable the Secretariat to fulfil its role as the main facilitator of the implementation of the Convention and the Strategic Framework (https://www.unccd.int/sites/default/files/inline-files/ICCD_COP%2813%29_L.18-1716078E_0.pdf).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to the Charter of the United Nations University (https://unu.edu/sites/default/files/2022-12/UNU-Charter-2014.pdf), the University's objectives are as follows: (1) To contribute, through collaborative research and education, to efforts to resolve the pressing global problems of human survival, development, and welfare that are the concern of the United Nations, its Peoples, and Member States (Article I, paragraph 1); (2) To disseminate the knowledge gained in its activities to the United Nations and its agencies, to scholars and to the public, in order to increase dynamic interaction in the worldwide community of learning and research (Article I, paragraph 4), (3) To assist in the development of vigorous academic and scientific communities everywhere and particularly in the developing countries, devoted to their vital needs in the fields of learning and research within the framework of the aims assigned to those centres and programmes in the present Charter (Article I, paragraph 6); and (4) To grant and confer master’s degrees and doctorates, diplomas, certificates and other academic distinctions under conditions laid down for that purpose in the statutes by the Council of the University (Article I, paragraph 8). These objectives reflect the University's mission as an international community of scholars, engaged in research, postgraduate training and dissemination of knowledge in furtherance of the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations (Article I, paragraph 1).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to the Ramsar Convention (https://www.ramsar.org/sites/default/files/documents/library/current_convention_text_e.pdf), Ramsar Secretariat’s objectives include the following key aspects: promoting the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands, recognizing their ecological, economic, cultural, and recreational value (Preamble; Article 3, paragraph 1); encouraging countries to identify and designate Wetlands of International Importance, which represent the best examples of wetland ecosystems of global significance (Article 2, paragraph 2); promoting international cooperation on wetland conservation and management, recognizing that the conservation of wetlands and their resources is a global concern that requires coordinated efforts (Article 5); equiring regular monitoring and reporting on the status of wetlands and their resources, the measures taken for their conservation and sustainable use, and the effectiveness of these measures (Article 3, paragraph 2; Article 6, paragraph 2 e); and promoting public awareness and education on the importance of wetlands and their conservation, recognizing that public support and involvement are essential for the success of wetland conservation efforts (Article 4, paragraph 3).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Article 1 of the Minamata Convention on Mercury (https://minamataconvention.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Minamata-Convention-booklet-Sep2019-EN.pdf), the objective of the Convention is to protect the human health and the environment from anthropogenic emissions and releases of mercury and mercury compounds. This objective is supported by provisions that relate to the entire life cycle of mercury, including controls and reductions across a range of products, processes and industries where mercury is used, released or emitted, as well as measures on the direct mining, trade, storage and disposal of mercury (https://minamataconvention.org/en/about). The Convention also addresses the impacts of mercury on vulnerable populations, especially women, children and indigenous communities, and provides for financial and technical assistance to developing countries and countries with economies in transition to implement the Convention (Article 13 and 14). Furthermore, the Convention establishes a mechanism for monitoring, reporting and reviewing the implementation and effectiveness of its provisions (Article 21 and 22).

Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to Part A, Section III of UNOOSA's working document "The 'Space2030' Agenda: Space as a Driver of Sustainable Development" (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2024/stspace/stspace88_0_html/st_space-088E.pdf), the United Nations UNOOSA has been mandated to fulfil the following objectives: Enhance space-derived economic benefits and strengthen the role of the space sector as a major driver of sustainable development (Overarching objective 1); Harness the potential of space to solve everyday challenges and leverage space-related innovation to improve the quality of life (Overarching objective 2); Improve access to space for all and ensure that all countries can benefit socioeconomically from space science and technology applications and space-based data, information and products, thereby supporting the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals (Overarching objective 3); and Build partnerships and strengthen international cooperation in the peaceful uses of outer space and in the global governance of outer space activities (Overarching objective 4). These objectives are structured around the four pillars of space economy, space society, space accessibility and space diplomacy, and are complemented by four core objectives that outline the specific actions to be taken by Member States, UNOOSA and other stakeholders to implement the "Space2030" Agenda (https://www.unoosa.org/res/oosadoc/data/documents/2024/stspace/stspace88_0_html/st_space-088E.pdf).

Methodological Notes: Keywords were extracted from the verbatim Defined Objectives text after removing URLs, non-alphanumeric characters, and common stopwords. This ensured the retention of only substantive thematic terms. Keywords were compared against an iteratively developed lexicon covering ten high-level representative strategies (Governance & Planning, Financial Stewardship, Policy & Regulation, Environmental Action, Knowledge & Data, Innovation & Technology, Inclusion & Rights, Partnerships & Networks, Operational Delivery, Monitoring & Accountability). Institution: United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC)
Defined Objectives (verbatim): According to the Secretary-General's bulletin ST/SGB/2004/6 (https://www.unodc.org/pdf/sgb_2004_6_unodc.pdf), UNODC has been mandated to fulfil the following objectives: Implementing the Organization's drug programme and crime programme in an integrated manner, addressing the interrelated issues of drug control, crime prevention and international terrorism in the context of sustainable development and human security (Section 2.1); Serving as the central drug control entity with exclusive responsibility for coordinating and providing effective leadership for all United Nations drug control activities and serving as the repository of technical expertise in international drug control for the Secretariat of the United Nations, including the regional commissions, and other United Nations organs, as well as Member States (Section 2.2 a); Acting on behalf of the Secretary-General in fulfilling his or her responsibilities under the terms of international treaties and resolutions of United Nations organs relating to international drug control (Section 2.2 b); Providing substantive services to the General Assembly, the Economic and Social Council and committees and conferences dealing with drug control matters (Section 2.2 c); Carrying out activities in the field of international crime prevention and control; strengthening regional and international cooperation in preventing and combating transnational crime, in particular organized and economic crime, money-laundering, illicit trafficking in women and children, financial crimes and terrorism in all its forms; and promoting effective and fair administration of justice, with due respect for the rights of all those affected by crime or involved in the criminal justice system (Section 2.3 a); Promoting adherence to the international treaties on drug control, crime prevention and terrorism and their effective implementation by States (Section 6.2 f); and Providing assistance to Member States in the implementation of relevant General Assembly resolutions and declarations related to action against terrorism (Section 6.2 g).
